meta.note: The band above competence: hedging, disagreeing politely, meetings, written register, money and admin, and the vocabulary of describing data. Units interleave so the unlock order stays varied. Examples are written for the deck — nothing here is quoted from anyone.

cards.trans: to check back on something after an earlier message or meeting
cards.note: follow up ON a matter, WITH a person; the noun is hyphenated: a follow-up
cards.ex_t: I'll follow up with the supplier on Monday if we still haven't heard back.

cards.trans: return to a topic, or to a person, later once something more urgent is done
cards.note: Business register and heavily overused, so save it for deferrals you actually intend to honour. The neutral alternative is 'come back to'.
cards.ex_t: Let's circle back to the pricing question once Marta has the final numbers.

cards.trans: to be doing or busy with something
cards.note: "What have you been up to?" is a standard opener — answer with an activity, not a feeling.
cards.ex_t: What have you been up to since we last spoke?

cards.trans: a warning attached to a claim, marking where it may not hold
cards.note: Collocations: attach a caveat, with the caveat that..., the usual caveats apply. Stress the first syllable, KAV-ee-at.
cards.ex_t: The uplift is real, but it comes with one caveat: we only have four weeks of data.

cards.trans: still not paid, or still waiting to be dealt with
cards.note: Looks like the praise word, but here it means unpaid. An 'outstanding balance' is money you owe, not money you have.
cards.ex_t: There are two outstanding invoices on the account, both from March.

cards.trans: to contact someone again about something they have not yet done or sent
cards.note: Separable: chase it up, chase up the referral. Americans say 'follow up on'.
cards.ex_t: If the clinic hasn't rung by Friday, I'll chase them up.

cards.trans: used to add a point that partly contradicts what you have just said
cards.note: 'That said' is the shorter, slightly more formal twin; both are fine in writing.
cards.ex_t: The model performed well last quarter; having said that, I wouldn't rely on it for the new market.

cards.trans: something that stops work going any further until it is resolved
cards.note: names the obstacle, not the person; say what is blocking you and who can clear it
cards.ex_t: The only blocker is access to the production database.

cards.trans: deliberately set a topic aside so the meeting can move on
cards.note: Usually 'park it for now'. It implies you will return to the topic, and people notice when you never do.
cards.ex_t: Can we park the naming debate and finish the roadmap first?

cards.trans: to want something or feel like having it
cards.note: The everyday British way to offer: Do you fancy...? Not used in this sense in American English.
cards.ex_t: Do you fancy a coffee before the meeting?

cards.trans: to make up a given share of a total; also, to allow for something in an analysis
cards.note: Two senses that live side by side. 'Accounts for 30%' = makes up. 'Once we account for seasonality' = adjust for. Context separates them.
cards.ex_t: Mobile users account for just under a third of all sessions.

cards.trans: to contact someone repeatedly to get money or an answer they owe you
cards.note: Normal office register, not aggressive. You chase an invoice, a payment or a person; 'chase them up' is slightly softer.
cards.ex_t: I'll chase the client again on Friday if the payment still hasn't landed.

cards.trans: to deal with a problem or arrange something so that it works
cards.note: Separable: sort it out, never 'sort out it'. Also passive-ish: I'll get it sorted.
cards.ex_t: The agency said they'd sort out the broken heater by Tuesday.

cards.trans: used to state something while admitting you may not have the full picture
cards.note: Covers you if you turn out to be wrong. The negative answer form is 'not that I'm aware of'.
cards.ex_t: As far as I'm aware, nobody has touched that table since March.

cards.trans: to be the person answerable for getting something done
cards.note: owning a task means being accountable for it, not doing every part yourself
cards.ex_t: Who owns the migration once the consultants leave?

cards.trans: interrupt a speaker briefly to add or correct something
cards.note: Soften it with 'sorry to' or 'can I just'. Without the softener it sounds abrupt on a call.
cards.ex_t: Sorry to jump in, but that deadline moved last week.

cards.trans: a warm but professional way to close an email
cards.note: The UK default. 'Regards' alone reads cooler, 'Best wishes' warmer; 'Yours sincerely' now belongs to formal letters.
cards.ex_t: I closed with 'Kind regards' rather than anything friendlier.

cards.trans: to leave a place
cards.note: Softer than "to leave" — announces your departure without sounding abrupt.
cards.ex_t: I'll head off around six if that's alright.

cards.trans: to confirm that a claim or an expectation was correct
cards.note: Often passive and often negative: 'that isn't borne out by the data'. Past participle is borne, not born.
cards.ex_t: The full quarter bears out what the early sample suggested.

cards.trans: to send someone a formal request for payment
cards.note: Used as a verb: invoice the client, invoice for the extra hours. 'Raise an invoice' means to create one.
cards.ex_t: We invoice at the end of every month and expect payment within thirty days.

cards.trans: to reply to someone later, once you have an answer
cards.note: 'I'll get back to you' is often a polite way of saying 'not now'.
cards.ex_t: The council took three weeks to get back to me about the permit.

cards.term: off the top of my head
cards.trans: from memory, without checking, so possibly not exact
cards.note: Buys thinking time and licenses an approximate number. Usually sits at the front of the answer.
cards.ex_t: Off the top of my head it's about forty thousand rows, but let me check.

cards.trans: the agreed boundaries of what a piece of work includes
cards.note: fixed phrases: in scope, out of scope, the scope of work
cards.ex_t: Let's agree the scope before anyone starts building.

cards.trans: disagree with a plan or request and say why, instead of simply accepting it
cards.note: Neutral and even valued in UK workplaces. The conditional 'I'd push back' is gentler than 'I push back'. Noun form: pushback.
cards.ex_t: I'd push back slightly on the timeline, because two weeks isn't enough for testing.

cards.trans: a polite marker that bad news or a refusal is coming
cards.note: Nothing to do with fear. It is the standard British softener for saying no in writing.
cards.ex_t: I'm afraid we can't take this on before September.

cards.trans: to do or spend free time on something
cards.note: The weekend question: What did you get up to at the weekend? British English says at the weekend, not on.
cards.ex_t: We didn't get up to much on Saturday.

cards.trans: compared with the same period twelve months earlier
cards.note: British form; Americans write year over year (YoY). Hyphenate before a noun: year-on-year growth.
cards.ex_t: Revenue is up eleven per cent year on year, and flat on the previous quarter.

cards.trans: to pay a bill or debt in full
cards.note: Formal, standard in letters from banks and utilities. 'Settle up' is the casual version between friends.
cards.ex_t: Please settle the balance before the end of the month to avoid interest.

cards.trans: please be patient for a moment while I do something
cards.note: Spelt 'bear', not 'bare'. Constant on the phone and at counters.
cards.ex_t: Bear with me while I pull your file up on the system.

cards.trans: used to accept that what someone said is valid before you answer it
cards.note: Nearly always followed by 'but' or 'though' — that pivot is what makes it polite rather than agreement.
cards.ex_t: I take your point about the deadline, though I'd still want to test it properly.

cards.trans: a specific piece of work you have agreed to hand over
cards.note: usually plural in plans: the deliverables for phase one
cards.ex_t: There are three deliverables in this phase, and the report is the first.

cards.trans: agree to discuss a side issue after the meeting, with fewer people
cards.note: 'Offline' here means 'not in this meeting'. It has nothing to do with being off the internet.
cards.ex_t: That's a database question, so shall we take it offline and report back on Thursday?

cards.trans: to be keen on something as an interest
cards.note: Informal; followed by a noun or an -ing form.
cards.ex_t: She's really into open-water swimming.

cards.trans: describing the real trend once one-off effects are stripped out
cards.note: Frequent pairs: underlying trend, underlying growth, underlying cause. Sits opposite headline.
cards.ex_t: Strip out the campaign spike and underlying demand is flat.

cards.trans: to pay someone back for money they have spent
cards.note: You reimburse a person, not a cost: reimburse me for the ticket, not reimburse the ticket. Noun: reimbursement.
cards.ex_t: The company will reimburse you for the taxi once you upload the receipt.

cards.trans: to connect a caller to another person or department by telephone
cards.note: From your side: I was put through to the wrong department. Related: hold the line.
cards.ex_t: I'll put you through to the billing team now.

cards.trans: used to introduce the problem or objection you are about to raise
cards.note: Signals bad news gently. Informal — good in meetings, weak in formal writing.
cards.ex_t: I'd love to help, but the thing is, I'm already covering two reports this week.

cards.trans: go back over the main points briefly so everyone has them clear
cards.note: Also a noun: 'a quick recap'. Opening with 'To recap' tells the room a summary is coming, not a new argument.
cards.ex_t: Before we finish, let me recap what each team has agreed to.

cards.trans: advance warning about something that is coming
cards.note: Hyphenated as a noun; you give someone a heads-up. Informal, so Slack and internal email only.
cards.ex_t: Just a heads-up: the dashboard will be down on Friday morning.

cards.trans: to have a friendly relationship with someone
cards.note: British; Americans say get along with. "Get on with it" is a different thing entirely — it means hurry up.
cards.ex_t: I get on with everyone on the analytics team.

cards.trans: to a degree large enough to change a decision
cards.note: Formal, common in reports and audit language. 'Not materially different' is a tactful way of saying the gap is real but irrelevant.
cards.ex_t: Excluding the outliers does not materially change the result.

cards.trans: to bring a cost, charge or penalty on yourself
cards.note: Formal, and the object is always something unwanted: costs, charges, fees, a penalty, interest.
cards.ex_t: Cancelling after the deadline will incur a fee of fifty euros.

cards.trans: to arrange an appointment or place for someone, especially at a clinic
cards.note: British; Americans say 'schedule'. You book someone in FOR something.
cards.ex_t: They booked me in for a scan on the 14th.

cards.trans: in general terms, without going into exceptions
cards.note: Same frame as 'roughly speaking' for numbers and 'strictly speaking' for precision.
cards.ex_t: Broadly speaking, users who sign up at the weekend churn faster.

cards.trans: to draw attention to a problem or point early
cards.note: BrE often adds up: flag it up in the meeting; it signals a risk, not blame
cards.ex_t: I'd rather flag the risk now than explain it in the review.

cards.trans: bring another person into a conversation or thread so they know what is happening
cards.note: Separable, and the pronoun must sit in the middle: loop her in, never 'loop in her'.
cards.ex_t: I'll loop Sofia in before we commit to a date.

cards.trans: to start leaving
cards.note: Usually "I'd better make a move" — the polite British signal that you are about to go.
cards.ex_t: It's getting late, so I'd better make a move.

cards.trans: to pull a figure or a sample in one direction and so distort it
cards.note: Also an adjective, skewed, and a noun. 'The sample skews young' means it leans young.
cards.ex_t: A handful of enterprise accounts skew the average basket size upwards.

cards.trans: money that is owed because payments were missed
cards.note: Always plural. 'Paid in arrears' also just means paid after the period worked, as with a monthly salary, and that sense is neutral.
cards.ex_t: Two missed payments and the account is already in arrears.

cards.trans: to move an appointment or event to an earlier date or time
cards.note: The opposite is 'push back' or 'put back'. American 'move up' also means earlier, which confuses everyone.
cards.ex_t: Can we bring the appointment forward to Monday morning?

cards.trans: an early warning that something is coming
cards.note: almost always with give: give someone a heads-up; informal but fine at work
cards.ex_t: Thanks for the heads-up about tomorrow's outage.

cards.trans: show an idea to someone informally to get their reaction before it is final
cards.note: Signals you want a reaction, not formal sign-off. 'Run it past someone' is the more common British variant.
cards.ex_t: Let me run the draft budget by finance before I present it.

cards.trans: thanks; also goodbye, or a toast
cards.note: Informal British. Fine with colleagues and in shops, too casual for a formal email.
cards.ex_t: Cheers for sorting that out so quickly.

cards.trans: to eliminate an explanation as impossible or unsupported
cards.note: Separable: rule it out. The weaker cousin, 'we can't rule out', is a standard hedge.
cards.ex_t: We can rule out a tracking bug, since the server logs show the same drop.

cards.trans: an arrangement letting a company take an agreed amount from your account automatically
cards.note: The company pulls a variable amount; a standing order is you pushing a fixed one. Neither term exists in American English.
cards.ex_t: I've set up a direct debit for the electricity so I stop forgetting it.

cards.trans: recorded in a letter or email rather than agreed only in speech
cards.note: The standard move once a complaint turns serious. Also 'put it in writing'.
cards.ex_t: Ask the landlord to confirm the rent reduction in writing.

cards.trans: a polite way of saying you have not understood and need it explained again
cards.note: Places the gap on you rather than the speaker, so nobody loses face. Far softer than 'that wasn't clear'.
cards.ex_t: I'm not sure I follow: is the discount applied before or after VAT?

cards.trans: to meet someone by chance
cards.ex_t: I bumped into an old colleague at the market.

cards.trans: a difference between two figures that ought to match
cards.note: Neutral and blame-free, which makes it safer than 'error' when you raise it with another team.
cards.ex_t: There is a small discrepancy between the billing export and the dashboard.

cards.trans: the part of an insurance claim you pay yourself before the insurer pays the rest
cards.note: British insurance term; Americans say deductible. A 'voluntary excess' lowers your premium in exchange for paying more per claim.
cards.ex_t: The repair came to eight hundred euros, but with a three-hundred euro excess the insurer only paid five.

cards.trans: the local family doctor who treats everyday problems and refers you onwards
cards.note: Short for general practitioner; say the letters. Register with a GP, see your GP.
cards.ex_t: You'll need to see a GP before the hospital will look at it.

cards.trans: used to restate what you have just said in clearer terms
cards.note: Useful when you see blank faces. 'Let me put it this way' is the more informal version.
cards.ex_t: The lift is real but tiny — to put it another way, we spent six weeks for half a percent.

cards.trans: to give final approval to a piece of work
cards.note: BrE often drops on: sign off the budget; the noun is sign-off
cards.ex_t: Nothing goes live until legal has signed off on the wording.

cards.trans: give someone the background they are missing so they can take part properly
cards.note: Separable, and the topic follows 'on'. 'Get up to speed' is the version you use about yourself.
cards.ex_t: Tiago has just joined the project, so I'll bring him up to speed on the migration.

cards.trans: a soft prompt about something that is overdue
cards.note: Many British readers hear it as passive-aggressive; 'just checking in on this' is safer.
cards.ex_t: She opened with a gentle reminder that the deadline was yesterday.

cards.trans: a polite way of ending a conversation
cards.note: Puts the leaving on you rather than on them, so it sounds considerate instead of bored.
cards.ex_t: Anyway, I won't keep you — enjoy the rest of your evening.

cards.trans: to work out why two sets of figures differ and bring them into agreement
cards.note: Pattern: reconcile A with or against B. The noun is reconciliation.
cards.ex_t: I spent the morning reconciling the finance numbers with our own totals.

cards.trans: the amount you pay for an insurance policy, usually monthly or yearly
cards.note: Not the adjective 'premium' meaning high-end. Premiums are quoted, they rise and fall, and you pay them.
cards.ex_t: My premium went up by thirty per cent after the claim.

cards.trans: the building or practice where a GP sees patients
cards.note: British trap: here it is not an operation. 'She's at the surgery' means at the doctor's.
cards.ex_t: The surgery opens at eight, so ring then for a same-day appointment.

cards.trans: used to admit a point is true before arguing that it doesn't matter much
cards.note: Sits at the front of the sentence with a comma. 'Admittedly' does the same job more formally.
cards.ex_t: Granted, the sample is small, but the pattern is hard to ignore.

cards.trans: the time and attention someone has spare for more work
cards.note: uncountable in this sense and slightly informal; keep it out of formal writing
cards.ex_t: I haven't got the bandwidth to take on another dashboard this week.

cards.trans: raise something so the group notices it now, without necessarily solving it
cards.note: British colleagues often say 'flag up'. Flagging is explicitly not the same as taking ownership, which is why it is useful.
cards.ex_t: I want to flag a risk: the supplier still hasn't confirmed the delivery date.

cards.trans: to prompt someone lightly about an unanswered request
cards.note: Warmer and lighter than 'chase'; very common in chat.
cards.ex_t: I'll nudge him again if there's nothing by Thursday.

cards.trans: to finally find the time to do something
cards.note: British spelling is round; followed by an -ing form: get round to booking.
cards.ex_t: I still haven't got round to booking the flights.

cards.trans: present in some places and missing in others; uneven in quality
cards.note: Very British and very useful for incomplete data or uneven results: patchy coverage, patchy adoption.
cards.ex_t: Coverage before 2023 is patchy, so I would not chart that period.

cards.trans: the protection an insurance policy gives you
cards.note: Uncountable in British English: cover for theft, never 'a cover'. Americans say coverage.
cards.ex_t: Check whether the policy includes cover for flooding before you sign.

cards.trans: an official request from one doctor for you to be seen by a specialist
cards.note: Verb: refer someone to. The document itself is a referral letter.
cards.ex_t: The dermatologist won't take you without a referral from your GP.

cards.trans: a mild way of saying you disagree or still have serious doubts
cards.note: British understatement: it usually means you disagree quite firmly.
cards.ex_t: I'm not entirely convinced the drop is seasonal.

cards.trans: to resist or question a request rather than simply accept it
cards.note: push back ON a request; a separate sense moves a date later: push the launch back
cards.ex_t: She pushed back on the timeline and asked for two more weeks.

cards.trans: a specific task agreed in a meeting, with an owner and usually a deadline
cards.note: British minutes use 'action point' or just 'action'; 'action item' is American. 'Action' is also used as a verb in offices ('who's actioning this?'), which is heavy jargon.
cards.ex_t: There are three action points from today and two of them are mine.

cards.trans: a brief, warm closing thank-you
cards.note: Works as a sign-off when you have asked for something; a shade warmer than 'Thanks'.
cards.ex_t: Many thanks for turning this around so quickly.

cards.trans: willing to join in with something
cards.note: Do not mix it up with "up to": Are you up for it? means willing, What are you up to? means doing.
cards.ex_t: Are you up for a walk on Sunday?

cards.trans: to stop rising and stay at roughly the same level
cards.note: Pronounced PLAT-oh in Britain. Also a noun: we've hit a plateau. Neighbours: level off, flatten out.
cards.ex_t: Sign-ups climbed for six weeks and then plateaued.

cards.trans: a stated price for a job or service, given before you agree to it
cards.note: Nothing to do with quoting words here. You get or request a quote; 'quotation' is the formal written version.
cards.ex_t: I got three quotes for the car insurance and the cheapest was half the price of the worst.

cards.trans: a renewal of regular medication issued without a new appointment
cards.note: British system term; the American equivalent is a 'refill'.
cards.ex_t: I've ordered my repeat prescription through the app.

cards.trans: work that has piled up and is still waiting to be done
cards.note: you clear, work through or prioritise a backlog
cards.ex_t: The backlog has grown faster than we can clear it.

cards.trans: bring a meeting or a topic to an end, usually with a short summary
cards.note: Noun form is hyphenated: 'a quick wrap-up'.
cards.ex_t: We're nearly out of time, so let's wrap up and take the rest by email.

cards.trans: a signal that you are closing a topic or a conversation
cards.note: Sentence-initial and with a falling tone it means "let's wrap this up", not "nevertheless".
cards.ex_t: Anyway, I should let you get back to work.

cards.trans: a small rise, especially after a flat or falling stretch
cards.note: Deliberately small; don't use it for a big jump. Opposite: a dip. Pattern: an uptick in something.
cards.ex_t: There is a modest uptick in weekend traffic, though it sits within normal variation.

cards.trans: the yearly form on which you declare your income to the tax office
cards.note: You file or submit a return. The return is the form; the money you get back is a refund or rebate.
cards.ex_t: I file my tax return in April, once the bank sends the interest statement.

cards.trans: sold in a pharmacy without a prescription
cards.note: Hyphenated before a noun: over-the-counter painkillers. OTC on packaging.
cards.ex_t: Ibuprofen is available over the counter, so you don't need to see anyone.

cards.trans: used after a number to show it is approximate
cards.note: Can carry the margin: 'give or take a week'. Spoken only — keep it out of reports.
cards.ex_t: The job runs in twenty minutes, give or take.

cards.trans: to raise an issue to someone more senior for a decision
cards.note: neutral, not aggressive; also intransitive, as in costs escalated quickly
cards.ex_t: If they miss the second deadline, we escalate it to their director.

cards.trans: to have enough spare time or capacity
cards.note: A polite way to refuse without writing a flat no.
cards.ex_t: I don't have the bandwidth to take this on this quarter.

cards.trans: to start a new hobby or activity
cards.ex_t: He took up bouldering after moving to the island.

cards.trans: to decrease gradually and then stop
cards.note: Gentler than drop or collapse: the fall is slow and smooth rather than sudden.
cards.ex_t: Interest in the feature tapers off after the first fortnight.

cards.trans: to accept that a debt will never be repaid, or to count a cost against taxable income
cards.note: Separable: write it off. A car damaged beyond repair is 'a write-off', hyphenated as a noun.
cards.ex_t: You can write off the laptop against tax if you use it mainly for work.

cards.trans: the queue of people waiting for a treatment or appointment
cards.note: You are ON a waiting list. 'Physio' is the normal short form of physiotherapy.
cards.ex_t: I'm on the waiting list for physio, apparently for four months.

cards.term: let me come back to you on that
cards.trans: used to postpone an answer you don't have yet
cards.note: Far better than inventing a number, but only if you actually do come back.
cards.ex_t: I don't want to guess the licence cost — let me come back to you on that.

cards.trans: the slow growth of a task beyond what was agreed
cards.note: uncountable; the usual verb is set in, as in scope creep has set in
cards.ex_t: Every extra chart they ask for is scope creep, and nobody is moving the deadline.

cards.term: see where someone is coming from
cards.trans: understand the reasoning behind what someone says, even when you don't agree with it
cards.note: Informal but safe in meetings. The continuous form is fixed: 'where you come from' means your home country, which is a different conversation entirely.
cards.ex_t: I can see where you're coming from, since you've been burned by a rushed launch before.

cards.trans: a casual British greeting, not a question about your health
cards.note: Answer "Yeah, you?" — reporting how you actually feel is the classic mistake here.
cards.ex_t: You alright? I haven't seen you in ages.

cards.trans: compared on the same basis, with known differences stripped out
cards.note: British retail and finance term; Americans say same-store or comparable. Hyphenated before a noun.
cards.ex_t: On a like-for-like basis the two regions are almost identical.

cards.trans: money given back to you because you paid too much
cards.note: A rebate comes back after overpayment; a discount is taken off up front. Usually 'tax rebate' or 'a rebate on the bill'.
cards.ex_t: I was on the wrong tax code all year, so a rebate should come through in June.

cards.trans: a doctor's statement about whether you are well enough to work
cards.note: Officially replaced 'sick note', though people still say sick note in conversation.
cards.ex_t: My GP gave me a fit note for two weeks.

cards.trans: used to agree partly but not completely
cards.note: A gentle brake. Said on its own with no follow-up it can sound dismissive.
cards.ex_t: That's true up to a point, though it breaks down for enterprise accounts.

cards.trans: outside the agreed boundaries of the work
cards.note: opposite of in scope; both follow the verb be
cards.ex_t: Anything before 2019 is out of scope for this analysis.

cards.trans: check quickly and informally that an idea or figure is reasonable before it goes further
cards.note: Chiefly British, and also a noun: 'a quick sense-check'. American colleagues say 'sanity check', which is falling out of favour.
cards.ex_t: Can I sense-check this with you? These figures look too good.

cards.trans: having no strong preference
cards.note: Warm and British; "I don't care" in the same slot sounds cold.
cards.ex_t: I'm not fussed where we eat, you choose.

cards.trans: a measurable stand-in for something you cannot measure directly
cards.note: Pattern: a proxy for X. Naming it out loud shows you know the measure is imperfect, which buys credibility.
cards.ex_t: We use session length as a proxy for engagement, which is crude but workable.

cards.trans: an amount you may earn or use before a rule or charge starts to apply
cards.note: In tax and travel this is a threshold, not pocket money: personal allowance, baggage allowance, mileage allowance.
cards.ex_t: The first slice of your income falls under the personal allowance and isn't taxed.

cards.trans: outside normal opening or working times
cards.note: Hyphenated before a noun: an out-of-hours service. Used for clinics, plumbers and helplines.
cards.ex_t: If it gets worse tonight, ring the out-of-hours number.

cards.trans: used to give the exact, technically correct version of something
cards.note: Can come across as pedantic if you use it to win small points.
cards.ex_t: Strictly speaking, it isn't a bug — the spec never covered that case.

cards.trans: the time needed to complete something and send it back
cards.note: one word as a noun: a quick turnaround; as a verb it splits: turn it around by Friday
cards.ex_t: They promise a two-day turnaround on any data request.

cards.trans: ask someone to keep an idea for a moment while something else is finished
cards.note: Friendly and slightly informal. It promises you will come back within the same meeting; for anything longer, use 'park'.
cards.ex_t: Hold that thought while we get the numbers on screen, then you can explain.

cards.trans: to show something to someone for their opinion before it goes out
cards.note: past, not passed. Americans say 'run by'.
cards.ex_t: Can I run the wording past you before I send it?

cards.trans: extremely tired
cards.note: Very informal British. Fine with friends, avoid with a client.
cards.ex_t: I was knackered after the hike, so we had an early night.

cards.trans: the level of detail at which data is recorded or reported
cards.note: Adjective: granular. 'Can we go more granular?' means can we break it down further.
cards.ex_t: We only have daily granularity, so the hourly question can't be answered.

cards.trans: left after tax and other deductions have been taken off
cards.note: Opposite of gross, the amount before deductions. Can follow the number: two thousand net.
cards.ex_t: The salary looks generous until you work out the net figure.

cards.trans: a company that rents out a property for the owner and deals with tenants
cards.note: British. 'To let' means for rent, hence the boards outside flats.
cards.ex_t: The letting agent takes a month's rent as a fee.

cards.trans: used to present a claim as defensible rather than certain
cards.note: Softens a bold claim; used on every sentence it makes you sound half-hearted.
cards.ex_t: This is arguably the cleanest dataset we have.

cards.trans: to fall behind a planned date
cards.note: dates and deadlines slip by themselves, with no object; the noun is slippage
cards.ex_t: The launch date has slipped twice already.

cards.trans: resolve the small problems or disagreements left in something broadly agreed
cards.note: Only for minor wrinkles. If the disagreement is fundamental, 'thrash out' or 'work through' is the honest choice.
cards.ex_t: The contract is basically settled; we just need to iron out the payment terms.

cards.trans: to give a particular impression, often without meaning to
cards.note: About how the reader receives it, not what you intended. This is the whole idea of tone in email.
cards.ex_t: That one-line reply comes across as colder than you meant.

cards.trans: a morning spent staying in bed later than usual
cards.note: You have a lie-in. Americans say sleep in.
cards.ex_t: The one thing I want at the weekend is a proper lie-in.

cards.trans: looking genuine but in fact false
cards.note: Formal. The standard pair is spurious correlation. Too strong for an honest slip: it implies the finding is worthless.
cards.ex_t: With enough variables you will find a spurious correlation sooner or later.

cards.trans: in proportion to the time or share involved
cards.note: Common in contracts and part-time adverts: 'thirty thousand pro rata' is the full-time rate scaled to your hours.
cards.ex_t: If you cancel halfway through the year, the fee is refunded pro rata.

cards.trans: the contract between tenant and landlord setting out rent and rules
cards.note: British for 'lease'. The tenancy is the arrangement; you are the tenant.
cards.ex_t: Read the tenancy agreement before you sign anything about pets.

cards.trans: to draw attention to something so that others can act on it
cards.note: British English also uses 'flag up'. The standard office verb for raising an issue without escalating it.
cards.ex_t: I'll flag the missing region codes to the data team this morning.

cards.trans: something your work cannot start or finish without
cards.note: a dependency ON something; in plans it is usually plural
cards.ex_t: Our only dependency is the new data feed, and it isn't ready.

cards.trans: make something vague definite, such as a date, a number or a commitment
cards.note: Also used of people: 'I couldn't nail him down to a date' means he kept avoiding the commitment.
cards.ex_t: Before we leave, can we nail down who is presenting on Monday?

cards.trans: so short that it sounds rude
cards.note: In British email the usual cause is a one-line reply with no greeting.
cards.ex_t: His answer was accurate but curt, so I softened the opening line.

cards.trans: slightly hungry
cards.note: British and understated — far milder than starving.
cards.ex_t: I'm getting a bit peckish — shall we find somewhere?

cards.trans: to treat two distinct things as if they were one
cards.note: Pattern: conflate A with B. Handy in review, and politer than telling someone they are confused.
cards.ex_t: The slide conflates new users with reactivated ones.

cards.trans: one of several smaller payments spread over time
cards.note: One 'l' in British spelling, two in American. The fixed phrase is 'pay in instalments'.
cards.ex_t: They let me pay the deposit in three monthly instalments.

cards.trans: how far in advance you must tell the other side you are ending an agreement
cards.note: Also used about jobs. 'Give notice' means formally announce you are leaving.
cards.ex_t: There's a two-month notice period, so tell them by the end of March.

cards.trans: after weighing both sides, taken as a whole
cards.note: Marks a conclusion after the pros and cons, so it shouldn't open the discussion.
cards.ex_t: On balance, I'd keep the old pipeline until the migration settles.

cards.trans: the one slow step that holds up everything after it
cards.note: about a stage or resource, not a person's character
cards.ex_t: Manual approval is the bottleneck, not the analysis.

cards.trans: add the missing detail to an idea that exists only in outline
cards.note: Watch the spelling. 'Flush out' means force something into the open and is a completely different verb.
cards.ex_t: The concept is good; flesh it out with costs and I'll take it to the board.

cards.trans: referring back to something already agreed in conversation
cards.note: 'As per our discussion' is stiffer and can read as building a case against the reader.
cards.ex_t: As discussed, I've attached the revised figures.

cards.trans: a polite way to end a conversation with someone who is busy
cards.note: "Get on" here means carry on with what they were doing.
cards.ex_t: Right, I'll let you get on — we'll speak next week.

cards.trans: a hidden third factor that drives both things you are comparing
cards.note: Also confounding variable, and the verb confound. 'Controlling for confounders' is the fixed phrase.
cards.ex_t: Region is an obvious confounder here: the two groups aren't drawn from the same market.

cards.trans: a single large payment made all at once
cards.note: The natural opposite of instalments; used for pensions, bonuses and annual subscriptions.
cards.ex_t: Paying the year up front as a lump sum works out about ten per cent cheaper.

cards.trans: the normal damage that comes from ordinary use over time
cards.note: Nearly always in the fixed phrase 'fair wear and tear' — what a landlord may not deduct from your deposit.
cards.ex_t: Faded paint is fair wear and tear, so they can't charge you for it.

cards.trans: used before a statement you believe is true, inviting the other person to correct it
cards.note: A polite way to challenge someone: you sound tentative while still making the point.
cards.ex_t: Correct me if I'm wrong, but this table hasn't refreshed since Friday.

cards.trans: a temporary way of getting past a problem without fixing it
cards.note: one word as a noun; the verb is two words: work around the problem
cards.ex_t: We have a workaround, but it won't survive the next release.

cards.trans: go over a list or a set of points quickly, from start to finish
cards.note: Noun form: 'a quick run-through'. 'Run through' is a fast preview; 'go through' suggests something slower and more thorough.
cards.ex_t: I'll run through the agenda first so you know what's coming.

cards.trans: a signal that the request is not urgent
cards.note: Takes the pressure off, but it will be taken literally, so add a real date if one exists.
cards.ex_t: Have a look when you get a chance; no rush.

cards.trans: to be received positively
cards.note: Works equally for food, jokes, news and presentations.
cards.ex_t: The dessert went down very well with everyone.

cards.trans: based on scattered individual reports rather than systematic evidence
cards.note: Anecdotal evidence is the set phrase. Mildly dismissive, so soften it: 'this is still anecdotal, but...'.
cards.ex_t: So far the complaints are anecdotal; I want to see whether the tickets back them up.

cards.trans: an agreement that continues automatically until one side ends it
cards.note: 'Rolling' is the key word: a rolling subscription rolls over each month. Compare 'fixed-term', which ends on a set date.
cards.ex_t: It's a rolling monthly contract, so you can leave whenever you like with thirty days' notice.

cards.trans: a term in a contract letting either side end it early
cards.note: You 'exercise' or 'trigger' a break clause. Common in rentals and phone contracts.
cards.ex_t: There's a break clause at six months if the job falls through.

cards.trans: used to skip the detail and jump to the outcome
cards.note: Keep the promise — whatever follows should genuinely be short.
cards.ex_t: Long story short, the join was duplicating rows.

cards.trans: to set something aside deliberately to return to it later
cards.note: in a meeting, park it means come back to it, not drop it
cards.ex_t: Can we park the pricing question until we have the numbers?

cards.trans: keep speaking while another person is speaking, so they cannot be heard
cards.note: Word order changes the meaning completely: 'talk something over' means discuss it properly, while 'talk over someone' is rude.
cards.ex_t: Sorry, I talked over you there. Please finish.

cards.trans: a chain of replies kept under one message or topic
cards.note: 'Reply in thread' means do not post it to the whole channel.
cards.ex_t: Let's keep this in the thread so the channel stays readable.

cards.trans: so tasty that you keep wanting more
cards.note: British; it compliments the food rather than criticising the eater.
cards.ex_t: Those little cheese pastries are dangerously moreish.

cards.trans: to choose only the cases that support your argument
cards.note: An accusation about method, not a word for an innocent mistake. Hyphenated in British usage.
cards.ex_t: If you cherry-pick the two best weeks, of course the campaign looks brilliant.

cards.trans: to continue for another period automatically unless you cancel
cards.note: Noun: auto-renewal. Usually the detail people miss: it auto-renewed and they were charged for another year.
cards.ex_t: The trial auto-renews into a yearly plan, so cancel before the tenth.

cards.trans: to work badly or cause trouble, of a device, a body part or a child
cards.note: British and informal, but fine with a landlord or a doctor: my knee's playing up again.
cards.ex_t: The boiler's been playing up since the cold snap.

cards.trans: used to offer an opinion while playing down its importance
cards.note: Modest on the surface, but often used to slip in a strong opinion.
cards.ex_t: For what it's worth, I'd run the test for another week.

cards.trans: the area of work someone is officially responsible for
cards.note: formal and distinctly British; the usual complaint is that's outside my remit
cards.ex_t: Pricing sits outside my remit, but I can point you to the right team.

cards.trans: of a voice on a call: become fragmented and hard to hear because the connection is poor
cards.note: Fixed in the continuous: 'you're breaking up'. Compare 'you cut out', where the sound disappeared altogether.
cards.ex_t: You're breaking up. Could you turn your camera off and try again?

cards.trans: to send a short message to get someone's attention
cards.note: Internal chat only. You would never write that you will ping a client.
cards.ex_t: Ping me when the export finishes.

cards.trans: having so many good options that choosing is hard
cards.note: British spelling spoilt; American English writes spoiled.
cards.ex_t: With three markets within walking distance, we're spoilt for choice.

cards.trans: not clear enough to settle the question either way
cards.note: Says the analysis was sound but the answer isn't there. Much weaker, and safer, than claiming no effect.
cards.ex_t: The test is inconclusive: the effect could be anywhere between nothing and six per cent.

cards.trans: unwanted moisture in the walls or structure of a building
cards.note: Uncountable noun as well as an adjective: 'we have damp' is normal. Related: mould (US mold), condensation.
cards.ex_t: There's damp behind the wardrobe and the plaster has gone black.

cards.trans: used to add a qualifying afterthought to what you have just said
cards.note: Strongly British and conversational; starts the qualifying clause or the next sentence.
cards.ex_t: It's much faster now — mind you, it hasn't had any real load yet.

cards.term: to be on the hook for
cards.trans: to be the one who will be blamed if something goes wrong
cards.note: informal; implies responsibility you did not necessarily want
cards.ex_t: If the figures are wrong, I'm on the hook for it, not the tool.

cards.trans: continue past the time something was supposed to finish
cards.note: Chiefly British; Americans say 'run over'. Stress the second syllable as a verb and the first as a noun ('a slight overrun').
cards.ex_t: The review overran by twenty minutes and I missed the start of your call.

cards.trans: lacking flavour or character
cards.note: Also used about films, design and writing.
cards.ex_t: The soup was warm but pretty bland.

cards.trans: to draw a bigger conclusion from something than it can support
cards.note: Nearly always negative or conditional: don't or wouldn't read too much into. A polite brake on an eager stakeholder.
cards.ex_t: I wouldn't read too much into a single week's dip.

cards.trans: to end a contract formally
cards.note: Legal register — for contracts and services, not for a meeting or a subscription you casually drop. In speech, use cancel or end.
cards.ex_t: Either side can terminate the agreement with sixty days' written notice.

cards.trans: to set something aside deliberately and return to it later
cards.note: Meeting shorthand: 'let's park that'. It sounds dismissive if the topic is never unparked.
cards.ex_t: Can we park the naming question and finish the schema first?

cards.trans: the passing of work and knowledge to whoever takes it on next
cards.note: one word as a noun, two as a verb: hand over the project
cards.ex_t: We've got one week for a proper handover before she leaves.

cards.trans: appear to be having one conversation while in fact meaning two different things
cards.note: Nearly always 'we're talking at cross purposes', which lets both sides retreat from a confused argument. 'Purposes' is always plural.
cards.ex_t: I think we're talking at cross purposes: I meant the client's deadline, not ours.

cards.trans: close of business, the end of the working day used as a deadline
cards.note: British-leaning; EOD is the American equivalent. Always add the time zone with spread-out teams.
cards.ex_t: Could you send the draft by COB Wednesday?

cards.trans: unpleasantly warm and humid
cards.ex_t: It's been muggy all week and I can't sleep.

cards.trans: a quick rough test that a number is not obviously wrong
cards.note: Also a verb: sanity-check the query. Informal but standard at work; some teams prefer 'quick check' in writing.
cards.ex_t: As a sanity check, the totals should add up to the figure on the invoice.

cards.trans: to choose not to charge or enforce something you had the right to
cards.note: Waive a fee, a charge, a requirement, your rights. Not the same word as 'wave'; the noun is waiver.
cards.ex_t: They waived the transfer fee because the delay was their fault.

cards.trans: the number shown on your gas, water or electricity meter, given to the supplier
cards.note: Verb: read the meter. Estimated bills are why this comes up so often.
cards.ex_t: Send them a meter reading or they'll carry on estimating the bill.

cards.trans: used to acknowledge a weakness in your own argument
cards.note: More formal than 'granted' and comfortable in written reports.
cards.ex_t: The method is slow, admittedly, but it's the only one we can audit.

cards.trans: argue the opposite case on purpose, to test how strong an idea really is
cards.note: Announce it before you argue, otherwise people assume the objection is genuinely yours.
cards.ex_t: Let me play devil's advocate for a second: what if users never find the new button?

cards.trans: to deal with a request
cards.note: A noun turned into a verb. Widespread in British offices, disliked by careful writers; 'deal with' is safer.
cards.ex_t: The request was actioned the same afternoon.

cards.trans: fine, light rain
cards.note: Also a verb: it's drizzling. In cooking it means to pour a thin stream of oil.
cards.ex_t: It's only drizzle, we can still walk down.

cards.trans: worked out roughly, without precision
cards.note: Used before a noun: a back-of-the-envelope figure. Flags honestly that the number is approximate.
cards.ex_t: A back-of-the-envelope estimate puts the saving at about two days a month.

cards.trans: legally forcing both sides to do what they agreed
cards.note: Usually 'legally binding'. 'Non-binding' marks a document as an intention only, such as a draft offer.
cards.ex_t: Once you tick the box and confirm, the quote becomes binding.

cards.trans: behind with payments that are already due
cards.note: Formal, common in letters. It also means paid at the end of a period: rent paid in arrears.
cards.ex_t: The account is two months in arrears, so they've frozen it.

cards.trans: used when something occurs to you as you are speaking
cards.note: Makes an idea sound spontaneous rather than prepared, which lowers the stakes of raising it.
cards.ex_t: Come to think of it, the same thing happened after the last release.

cards.trans: drift away from the topic into something only loosely related
cards.note: The older British form is 'go off at a tangent' and is still heard. Useful when steering a meeting back: 'I've gone off on a tangent, sorry.'
cards.ex_t: We went off on a tangent about hiring and never got back to the budget.

cards.trans: to rain very heavily
cards.note: Informal British and always with "it": it's chucking it down.
cards.ex_t: We got to the door just as it started chucking it down.

cards.trans: a factor of roughly ten; the rough scale of a number rather than its exact size
cards.note: 'An order of magnitude larger' means about ten times larger. Don't stretch it to mean 'a bit bigger'.
cards.ex_t: We only need the order of magnitude here: is it hundreds or thousands?

cards.trans: the detailed conditions of a contract, where the awkward rules sit
cards.note: British; Americans say 'the fine print'. Normally with read or check, and it implies something unwelcome is buried there.
cards.ex_t: The offer looked great until I read the small print and found the exit fee.

cards.trans: to add money or credit to something so it is full again
cards.note: British; the noun is 'a top-up'. Used for phone credit, travel cards and drinks too.
cards.ex_t: I need to top up the electricity key before the weekend.

cards.trans: used before restating something to remove any misunderstanding
cards.note: Tone-sensitive: delivered flatly it reads as a correction or a warning shot.
cards.ex_t: Just to be clear, we're only changing the weekly view, not the daily one.

cards.trans: extra time built into a plan in case something goes wrong
cards.note: the usual collocation is build in a buffer
cards.ex_t: There's no buffer in this plan, so one bad week sinks it.

cards.trans: discuss a difficult issue at length until an agreement is reached
cards.note: Chiefly British, and the tone implies real effort. Americans say 'hash out' for the same thing.
cards.ex_t: We spent the whole afternoon thrashing out who owns the data.

cards.trans: a formal way to introduce a file you are sending
cards.note: Old-fashioned. 'I've attached the contract' reads better in modern British email.
cards.ex_t: Please find attached the signed contract.

cards.trans: to become sunnier, or more cheerful
cards.note: Used of weather, of rooms and of people.
cards.ex_t: They reckon it'll brighten up by lunchtime.

cards.trans: the single number quoted publicly, before any adjustment
cards.note: British reporting language and the natural opposite of underlying. Also headline rate, headline number.
cards.ex_t: The headline figure is forty per cent growth; the like-for-like number is nearer twelve.

cards.trans: a document showing where you live, required to open accounts
cards.note: Usually a recent utility bill or bank statement. Goes with 'proof of identity' and 'photo ID'.
cards.ex_t: They wouldn't open the account without proof of address dated in the last three months.

cards.trans: used to specify exactly who or what you mean
cards.note: Introduces the complete list; 'such as' introduces examples only.
cards.ex_t: Two markets are dragging the average down, namely Spain and Poland.

cards.trans: to have far more work than you can reasonably handle
cards.note: British and informal; snowed under WITH work, and always passive
cards.ex_t: I'm snowed under until Thursday, so anything new will have to wait.

cards.trans: have doubts you are prepared to state, without rejecting the idea outright
cards.note: Formal and measured, and it survives well in written minutes. Usually 'some reservations' or 'serious reservations'.
cards.ex_t: I have reservations about launching in August, though I won't block it.

cards.trans: as soon as you reasonably can
cards.note: Polite but distant and vague. If you need a date, write the date.
cards.ex_t: Please confirm the figures at your earliest convenience.

cards.trans: pleasantly not cold for the season
cards.note: In weather talk it is a compliment; about food the same word means not spicy.
cards.ex_t: It's been a very mild winter here.

cards.trans: to hide a real pattern behind a summary figure
cards.note: 'The average masks...' is a workhorse opening for any analyst. Near neighbours: obscure, conceal.
cards.ex_t: The flat average masks a sharp split between new and returning customers.

cards.trans: to approve something officially, usually spending or a document
cards.note: In this sense it takes 'on': sign off on the budget. Bare 'sign off' can also mean ending a message, or in Britain being declared unfit for work.
cards.ex_t: Finance has to sign off on any purchase over a thousand euros.

cards.trans: to have an official right to something
cards.note: Officialese, everywhere in letters. But calling a person 'entitled' is an insult: they think they deserve special treatment.
cards.ex_t: As a resident you're entitled to the same cover as anyone else.

cards.trans: to sort tasks by urgency before deciding what to do
cards.note: borrowed from medicine; it means sorting, not solving
cards.ex_t: Let's triage the requests first and see what actually needs doing this week.

cards.trans: a formal opening that signals firm disagreement, usually with someone more senior
cards.note: A trap. It sounds courteous but almost always precedes a blunt contradiction, and British listeners often hear it as combative. 'I'd see it slightly differently' is safer.
cards.ex_t: With all due respect, the figures in that report are three months old.

cards.trans: at some suitable point later, with no date promised
cards.note: A British hedge: the reader will correctly hear 'not soon'.
cards.ex_t: We'll share the full results in due course.

cards.trans: an evening or weekend spent doing very little
cards.note: Usually "we had a quiet one" — a normal, positive answer to the weekend question.
cards.ex_t: We had a quiet one, just a film and an early night.

cards.trans: to cancel out part or all of a movement in the opposite direction
cards.note: Usually passive: X was offset by Y. Stress differs by word class: OFF-set the noun, off-SET the verb.
cards.ex_t: Losses in the north were offset by a strong quarter in Lisbon.

cards.trans: having taken more money out of an account than it contained
cards.note: Adjective for you or the account; the arrangement itself is 'an overdraft'. Informally, 'in the red'.
cards.ex_t: The subscription went out before payday and left me overdrawn.

cards.trans: used to introduce a thought that undercuts what you have just said
cards.note: Signals thinking aloud, which makes a change of position sound reasonable rather than inconsistent.
cards.ex_t: We could rebuild it properly — then again, nobody has opened that report in months.

cards.term: to get something over the line
cards.trans: to finish something that is almost complete
cards.note: British; suits the last push on a project, not the start of one
cards.ex_t: One more review and we can get this over the line.

cards.trans: in British usage, to put a proposal forward formally for discussion
cards.note: A genuine transatlantic trap: in American English, tabling something means postponing it indefinitely, the opposite meaning. On mixed calls, say 'put forward' or 'postpone' and avoid the word.
cards.ex_t: The finance team tabled a revised budget at yesterday's board meeting.

cards.term: I hope this finds you well
cards.trans: a neutral opening pleasantry in an email
cards.note: Harmless but empty; British colleagues will not miss it if you go straight to the point.
cards.ex_t: I hope this finds you well. I'm writing about next month's workshop.

cards.trans: to spend time on small, unhurried tasks
cards.note: British; potter around is equally correct. Americans say putter.
cards.ex_t: I spent Sunday pottering about in the garden.

cards.trans: a consequence that follows indirectly from an earlier change
cards.note: British; Americans say ripple effect. Knock-on also works as an adjective: knock-on costs, knock-on delays.
cards.ex_t: The pricing change had a knock-on effect on support volumes.

cards.trans: to compare prices from several providers before buying
cards.note: Phrasal verb with no object: shop around for car insurance. Standard advice about insurance, energy and mobile plans.
cards.ex_t: Shop around before the policy renews instead of accepting whatever price they send you.

cards.trans: an independent official who investigates complaints against companies or public bodies
cards.note: Usually free, and only available once the company's own complaints process is exhausted.
cards.ex_t: If they reject the claim, take it to the ombudsman.

cards.trans: if it is really necessary, though it would be a stretch
cards.note: British; it warns that you are agreeing at the very limit of what's possible.
cards.ex_t: I could have a draft ready by Thursday at a push.

cards.trans: a feature that would be welcome but is not required
cards.note: hyphenated as a noun and usually set against a must-have
cards.ex_t: Real-time refresh is a nice-to-have, not a requirement.

cards.trans: any other business: the slot near the end of an agenda for items nobody listed in advance
cards.note: Standard on British agendas and minutes, said as three separate letters. With an international group, say the full 'any other business' at least once.
cards.ex_t: We've got five minutes for AOB if anyone has something short.

cards.trans: to choose the exact way something is expressed
cards.note: Use this, not 'formulate', which sounds academic. The noun is the wording.
cards.ex_t: I'd word that last paragraph more carefully.

cards.trans: to like each other immediately
cards.note: Add with for the other person: they hit it off with the new team.
cards.ex_t: We hit it off straight away and talked for an hour.

cards.term: take with a pinch of salt
cards.trans: to treat something as unreliable and not act on it fully
cards.note: British form; Americans say a grain of salt. Fine spoken in a meeting, too casual for a written report.
cards.ex_t: Take the first day of data with a pinch of salt, as the tagging was still settling.

cards.trans: personally worse off in money terms after paying for something
cards.note: British usage is strictly about losing your own money. In American English it can also mean unreachable, which causes real confusion by email.
cards.ex_t: If the refund never arrives, I'm forty euros out of pocket.

cards.trans: to draw attention to a problem early so that it is not missed
cards.note: British; Americans say 'flag' or 'raise'. Useful when you want proof that you warned someone.
cards.ex_t: I flagged up the damp when I moved in, and it's all in the email.
